# Peer review - Round 1

Reviewers:
- Anonymous Reviewer

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92525.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92525.3.sa3)

This manuscript by Akabuogu et al. investigates membrane potential dynamics in E. coli. Membrane potential fluctuations have been observed in bacteria by several research groups in recent years, including in the context of bacterial biofilms where they have been proposed to play a role in cellular communication. Here, these authors investigate membrane potential in E. coli, in both single cells and biofilms. I have reviewed the revised manuscript provided by the authors, as well as their responses to the initial reviews; my opinion about the manuscript is largely unchanged. I have focused my public review on those issues that I believe to be most pressing, with additional comments included in the review to authors. Although these authors are working in an exciting research area, the evidence they provide for their claims is inadequate, and several key control experiments are still missing. In some cases, the authors allude to potentially relevant data in their responses to the initial reviews, but unfortunately these data are not shown. Furthermore, I cannot identify any traveling wavefronts in the data included in this manuscript. In addition to the challenges associated with the use of Thioflavin-T (ThT) raised by the second reviewer, these caveats make the work presented in this manuscript difficult to interpret.

First, some of the key experiments presented in the paper lack required controls:

(1) This paper asserts that the observed ThT fluorescence dynamics are induced by blue light. This is a fundamental claim in the paper, since the authors go on to argue that these dynamics are part of a blue light response. This claim must be supported by the appropriate negative control experiment measuring ThT fluorescence dynamics in the absence of blue light- if this idea is correct, these dynamics should not be observed in the absence of blue light exposure. If this experiment cannot be performed with ThT since blue light is used for its excitation, TMRM can be used instead.

In response to this, the authors wrote that ‘the fluorescent baseline is too weak to measure cleanly in this experiment.’ If they observe no ThT signal above noise in their time lapse data in the absence of blue light, this should be reported in the manuscript- this would be a satisfactory negative control. They then wrote that ‘It appears the collective response of all the bacteria hyperpolarization at the same time appears to dominate the signal.’ I am not sure what they mean by this- perhaps that ThT fluorescence changes strongly only in response to blue light? This is a fundamental control for this experiment that ought to be presented to the reader.

(2) The authors claim that a ∆kch mutant is more susceptible to blue light stress, as evidenced by PI staining. The premise that the cells are mounting a protective response to blue light via these channels rests on this claim. However, they do not perform the negative control experiment, conducting PI staining for WT the ∆kch mutant in the absence of blue light. In the absence of this control it is not possible to rule out effects of the ∆kch mutation on overall viability and/or PI uptake. The authors do include a growth curve for comparison, but planktonic growth is a very different context than surface-attached biofilm growth. Additionally, the ∆kch mutation may have impacts on PI permeability specifically that are not addressed by a growth curve. The negative control experiment is of key importance here.

Second, the ideas presented in this manuscript rely entirely on analysis of ThT fluorescence data, specifically a time course of cellular fluorescence following blue light treatment. However, alternate explanations for and potential confounders of the observed dynamics are not sufficiently addressed:

(1) Bacterial cells are autofluorescent, and this fluorescence can change significantly in response to stress (e.g. blue light exposure). To characterize and/or rule out autofluorescence contributions to the measurement, the authors should present time lapse fluorescence traces of unstained cells for comparison, acquired under the same imaging conditions in both wild type and ∆kch mutant cells. In their response to reviewers the authors suggested that they have conducted this experiment and found that the autofluorescence contribution is negligible, which is good, but these data should be included in the manuscript along with a description of how these controls were conducted.

(2) Similarly, in my initial review I raised a concern about the possible contributions of photobleaching to the observed fluorescence dynamics. This is particularly relevant for the interpretation of the experiment in which catalase appears to attenuate the decay of the ThT signal; this attenuation could alternatively be due to catalase decreasing ThT photobleaching. In their response, the authors indicated that photobleaching is negligible, which would be good, but they do not share any evidence to support this claim. Photobleaching can be assessed in this experiment by varying the light dosage (illumination power, frequency, and/or duration) and confirming that the observed fluorescence dynamics are unaffected.

Third, the paper claims in two instances that there are propagating waves of ThT fluorescence that move through biofilms, but I do not observe these waves in any case:

(1) The first wavefront claim relates to small cell clusters, in Fig. 2A and Video S2 and S3 (with Fig. 2A and Video S2 showing the same biofilm.) I simply do not see any evidence of propagation in either case- rather, all cells get brighter and dimmer in tandem. I downloaded and analyzed Video S3 in several ways (plotting intensity profiles for different regions at different distances from the cluster center, drawing a kymograph across the cluster, etc.) and in no case did I see any evidence of a propagating wavefront. (I attempted this same analysis on the biofilm shown in Fig. 2A and Video S2 with similar results, but the images shown in the figure panels and especially the video are still both so saturated that the quantification is difficult to interpret.) If there is evidence for wavefronts, it should be demonstrated explicitly by analysis of several clusters. For example, a figure of time-to-peak vs. position in the cluster demonstrating a propagating wave would satisfy this. Currently, I do not see any wavefronts in this data.

(2) The other wavefront claim relates to biofilms, and the relevant data is presented in Fig. S4 (and I believe also in what is now Video S8, but no supplemental video legends are provided, and this video is not cited in text.) As before, I cannot discern any wavefronts in the image and video provided; Reviewer 1 was also not able to detect wave propagation in this video by kymograph. Some mean squared displacements are shown in Fig. 7. As before, the methods for how these were obtained are not clearly documented either in this manuscript or in the BioRXiv preprint linked in the initial response to reviewers, and since wavefronts are not evident in the video it is hard to understand what is being measured here- radial distance from where? (The methods section mentions radial distance from the substrate, this should mean Z position above the imaging surface, and no wavefronts are evident in Z in the figure panels or movie.) Thus, clear demonstration of these wavefronts is still missing here as well.

Fourth, I have some specific questions about the study of blue light stress and the use of PI as a cell viability indicator:

(1) The logic of this paper includes the premise that blue light exposure is a stressor under the experimental conditions employed in the paper. Although it is of course generally true that blue light can be damaging to bacteria, this is dependent on light power and dosage. The control I recommended above, staining cells with PI in the presence and absence of blue light, will also allow the authors to confirm that this blue light treatment is indeed a stressor- the PI staining would be expected to increase in the presence of blue light if this is so.

(2) The presence of ThT may complicate the study of the blue light stress response, since ThT enhances the photodynamic effects of blue light in E. coli (Bondia et al. 2021 Chemical Communications). The authors could investigate ThT toxicity under these conditions by staining cells with PI after exposing them to blue light with or without ThT staining.

(3) In my initial review, I wrote the following: "In Figures 4D - E, the interpretation of this experiment can be confounded by the fact that PI uptake can sometimes be seen in bacterial cells with high membrane potential (Kirchhoff & Cypionka 2017 J Microbial Methods); the interpretation is that high membrane potential can lead to increased PI permeability. Because the membrane potential is largely higher throughout blue light treatment in the ∆kch mutant (Fig. 3[BC]), this complicates the interpretation of this experiment." In their response, the authors suggested that these results are not relevant in this case because "In our experiment methodology, cell death was not forced on the cells by introducing an extra burden or via anoxia." However, the logic of the paper is that the cells are in fact dying due to an imposed external stressor, which presumably also confers an increased burden as the cells try to deal with the stress. Instead, the authors should simply use a parallel method to confirm the results of PI staining. For example, the experiment could be repeated with other stains, or the viability of blue light-treated cells could be addressed more directly by outgrowth or colony-forming unit assays.

The CFU assay suggested above has the additional advantage that it can also be performed on planktonic cells in liquid culture that are exposed to blue light. If, as the paper suggests, a protective response to blue light is being coordinated at the biofilm level by these membrane potential fluctuations, the WT strain might be expected to lose its survival advantage vs. the ∆kch mutant in the absence of a biofilm.

Fifth, in several cases the data are presented in a way that are difficult to interpret, or the paper makes claims that are different to observe in the data:

(1) The authors suggest that the ThT and TMRM traces presented in Fig. S1D have similar shapes, but this is not obvious to me- the TMRM curve has very little decrease after the initial peak and only a modest, gradual rise thereafter. The authors suggest that this is due to increased TMRM photobleaching, but I would expect that photobleaching should exacerbate the signal decrease after the initial peak. Since this figure is used to support the use of ThT as a membrane potential indicator, and since this is the only alternative measurement of membrane potential presented in text, the authors should discuss this discrepancy in more detail.

(2) The comparison of single cells to microcolonies presented in figures 1B and D still needs revision:

First, both reviewer 1 and I commented in our initial reviews that the ThT traces, here and elsewhere, should not be normalized- this will help with the interpretation of some of the claims throughout the manuscript.

Second, the way these figures are shown with all traces overlaid at full opacity makes it very difficult to see what is being compared. Since the point of the comparison is the time to first peak (and the standard deviation thereof), histograms of the distributions of time to first peak in both cases should be plotted as a separate figure panel.

Third, statistical significance tests ought to be used to evaluate the statistical strength of the comparisons between these curves. The authors compare both means and standard deviations of the time to first peak, and there are appropriate statistical tests for both types of comparisons.

(3) The authors claim that the curve shown in Fig. S4B is similar to the simulation result shown in Fig. 7B. I remain unconvinced that this is so, particularly with respect to the kinetics of the second peak- at least it seems to me that the differences should be acknowledged and discussed. In any case, the best thing to do would be to move Fig. S4B to the main text alongside Fig. 7B so that the readers can make the comparison more easily.

(4) As I wrote in my first review, in the discussion of voltage-gated calcium channels, the authors refer to "spiking events", but these are not obvious in Figure S3E. Although the fluorescence intensity changes over time, these fluctuations cannot be distinguished from measurement noise. A no-light control could help clarify this.

(5) In the lower irradiance conditions in Fig. 4A, the ThT dynamics are slower overall, and it looks like the ThT intensity is beginning to rise at the end of the measurement. The authors write that no second peak is observed below an irradiance threshold of 15.99 µW/mm2. However, could a more prominent second peak be observed in these cases if the measurement time was extended? Additionally, the end of these curves looks similar to the curve in Fig. S4B, in which the authors write that the slow rise is evidence of the presence of a second peak, in contrast to their interpretation here.

Additional considerations:

(1) The analysis and interpretation of the first peak, and particularly of the time-to-fire data is challenging throughout the manuscript the time resolution of the data set is quite limited. It seems that a large proportion of cells have already fired after a single acquisition frame. It would be ideal to increase the time resolution on this measurement to improve precision. This could be done by imaging more quickly, but that would perhaps necessitate more blue light exposure; an alternative is to do this experiment under lower blue light irradiance where the first spike time is increased (Figure 4A).

(2) The authors suggest in the manuscript that "E. coli biofilms use electrical signalling to coordinate long-range responses to light stress." In addition to the technical caveats discussed above, I am missing a discussion about what these responses might be. What constitutes a long-range response to light stress, and are there known examples of such responses in bacteria?

(3) The presence of long-range blue light responses can also be interrogated experimentally, for example, by repeating the Live/Dead experiment in planktonic culture or the single-cell condition. If the protection from blue light specifically emerges due to coordinated activity of the biofilm, the ∆kch mutant would not be expected to show a change in Live/Dead staining in non-biofilm conditions. The CFU experiment I mentioned above could also implicate coordinated long-range responses specifically, if biofilms and liquid culture experiments can be compared (although I know that recovering cells from biofilms is challenging.)

4. At the end of the results section, the authors suggest a critical biofilm size of only 4 μm for wavefront propagation (not much larger than a single cell!) The authors show responses for various biofilm sizes in Fig. 2C, but these are all substantially larger (and this figure also does not contain wavefront information.) Are there data for cell clusters above and below this size that could support this claim more directly?

(5) In Fig. 4C, the overall trajectories of extracellular potassium are indeed similar, but the kinetics of the second peak of potassium are different than those observed by ThT (it rises minutes earlier)- is this consistent with the idea that Kch is responsible for that peak? Additionally, the potassium dynamics also include the first ThT peak- is this surprising given that the Kch channel has no effect on this peak according to the model?

Detailed comments:

Why are Fig. 2A and Video S2 called a microcluster, whereas Video S3, which is smaller, is called a biofilm?

"We observed a spontaneous rapid rise in spikes within cells in the center of the biofilm" (Line 140): What does "spontaneous" mean here?

"This demonstrates that the ion-channel mediated membrane potential dynamics is a light stress relief process.", "E. coli cells employ ion-channel mediated dynamics to manage ROS-induced stress linked to light irradiation." (Line 268 and the second sentence of the Fig. 4F legend): This claim is not well-supported. There are several possible interpretations of the catalase experiment (which should be discussed); this experiment perhaps suggests that ROS impacts membrane potential but does not indicate that these membrane potential fluctuations help the cells respond to blue light stress. The loss of viability in the ∆kch mutant might indicate a link between these membrane potential experiments and viability, but it is hard to interpret without the no light controls I mention above.

"The model also predicts... the external light stress" (Lines 338-341): Please clarify this section. Where does this prediction arise from in the modeling work? Second, I am not sure what is meant by "modulates the light stress" or "keeps the cell dynamics robust to the intensity of external light stress" (especially since the dynamics clearly vary with irradiance, as seen in Figure 4A).

"We hypothesized that E. coli not only modulates the light-induced stress but also handles the increase of the ROS by adjusting the profile of the membrane potential dynamics" (Line 347): I am not sure what "handles the ROS by adjusting the profile of the membrane potential dynamics" means. What is meant by "handling" ROS? Is the hypothesis that membrane potential dynamics themselves are protective against ROS, or that they induce a ROS-protective response downstream, or something else? Later the authors write that changes in the response to ROS in the model agree with the hypothesis, but just showing that ROS impacts the membrane potential does not seem to demonstrate that this has a protective effect against ROS.

"Mechanosensitive ion channels (MS) are vital for the first hyperpolarization event in E. coli." (Line 391): This is misleading- mechanosensitive ion channels totally ablate membrane potential dynamics, they don't have a specific effect on the first hyperpolarization event. The claim that mechanonsensitive ion channels are specifically involved in the first event also appears in the abstract.

Also, the apparent membrane potential is much lower even at the start of the experiment in these mutants (Fig. 6C-D)- is this expected? This seems to imply that these ion channels also have a blue light-independent effect.

Throughout the paper, there are claims that the initial ThT spike is involved in "registering the presence of the light stress" and similar. What is the evidence for this claim?

"We have presented much better quantitative agreement of our model with the propagating wavefronts in E. coli biofilms..." (Line 619): It is not evident to me that the agreement between model and prediction is "much better" in this work than in the cited work (reference 57, Hennes et al. 2023). The model in Figure 4 of ref. 57 seems to capture the key features of their data.

In methods, "Only cells that are hyperpolarized were counted in the experiment as live" (Line 745): what percentage of cells did not hyperpolarize in these experiments?

Some indication of standard deviation (error bars or shading) should be added to all figures where mean traces are plotted.

Video S8 is very confusing- why does the video play first forwards and then backwards? It is easy to misinterpret this as a rise in the intensity at the end of the experiment.

results.result: E. coli biofilms exhibit synchronized membrane potential dynamics with two distinct hyperpolarization events in response to blue light stress. Single cells show a cell-wide rise in fluorescence intensity, followed by quiescence, then a slow increase persisting for 60 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C32, C37, and C115 collectively demonstrate synchronized membrane potential dynamics in E. coli biofilms with two hyperpolarization peaks. The experimental data from ThT fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1B, Figure 2B) provides direct visual and quantitative evidence for these dynamics across single cells, microclusters, and mature biofilms.

results.result: The first hyperpolarization event requires mechanosensitive ion channels (MscK, MscL, and MscS). Deletion mutants lacking these MS channels show no spike dynamics, and the unknown channel Q is connected with MS channels to propagate the initial spike.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C33, C97, C98, C132, and C133 are supported by genetic deletion experiments (Figure 6C, 6D) showing that ΔMscK, ΔMscS, and ΔMscL mutants lack the typical spiking dynamics observed in wildtype cells. The complementation and phenotype confirmation across strains strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: The second hyperpolarization event depends on the Kch potassium channel, which controls refractoriness and habituation. Deletion of Kch eliminates the second peak while preserving the first, and complementation restores wildtype dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C34, C66-C69, C123-C124 are strongly supported by genetic experiments showing Δkch mutants lack the second peak (Figure 3B, 3C, Appendix 1-figure 3C), complementation restores the phenotype (Appendix 1-figure 3D), and this pattern is consistent across strains. The LiveDead assay (C77-C80) further supports Kch's functional importance.

results.result: Electrical signaling synchronization increases with cell density. Sparse cells show high variability (7.34±10.89 min to first peak), microclusters show reduced variability (3.24±1.77 min), and biofilms show the fastest and most synchronized response (2.73±0.85 min).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47, C55-C57, C84, and C116 are supported by quantitative measurements (Figure 1E, Appendix 1-figure 3B) showing progressive reduction in latency and variability as intercellular distance decreases. The statistical data with mean±SD±SE values provide robust evidence for density-dependent synchronization.

results.result: E. coli biofilms exhibit coordinated ion-channel-mediated wavefronts that propagate from center to edges (centrifugal), collapse back to center (centripetal), undergo quiescence, then re-emerge and persist at the periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54, C61-C62 describe the spatiotemporal dynamics of wavefront propagation supported by time-lapse microscopy (Figure 2A, Video 3). The detailed description of bidirectional wavefront movement with intervening quiescence is directly observable in the experimental data.

results.result: Extracellular potassium ion changes mirror the ThT membrane potential dynamics, showing a sharp rise, quiescence period, and plateau, indicating K+ ions play a vital role in the observed dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by direct measurement using IPG-4 potassium indicator (Figure 4C) showing temporal correlation between extracellular K+ changes and membrane potential dynamics. This provides mechanistic evidence for potassium-based signaling.

results.result: Light irradiance modulates membrane potential dynamics in a dose-dependent manner. All irradiances produce a first peak with decreasing latency at higher intensities, but only above 15.99 µW/mm² threshold does the second peak occur with progressively faster kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 and C138 are supported by systematic irradiance experiments (Figure 4A, 4B) showing quantitative relationships between light intensity and response kinetics. The identification of a threshold irradiance for the second peak provides important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Wildtype E. coli with intact Kch channels show significantly better survival under blue light stress (1.7% PI-positive) compared to Δkch mutants (7.6% PI-positive), demonstrating that ion-channel-mediated membrane potential dynamics help cells withstand light stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 and C144 are supported by LiveDead assay with propidium iodide staining (Figure 4D, 4E) and statistical analysis (Student's t-test, p≤0.05). The ~4.5-fold difference in cell damage provides functional evidence for the protective role of Kch-mediated dynamics.

results.result: Addition of catalase (ROS scavenger) eliminates the second hyperpolarization event while preserving the first peak, demonstrating that the ion-channel-mediated dynamics is a light stress relief process responding to accumulating ROS.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 and C87 are supported by catalase experiments (Figure 4F, Video 5) showing selective elimination of the second peak. This provides mechanistic evidence linking ROS accumulation to the second hyperpolarization event and supports the stress relief interpretation.

results.result: A Hodgkin-Huxley conductance model with two voltage-gated ion channels (Q and Kch) successfully reproduces the experimental membrane potential dynamics. Channel Q activates faster but deactivates slower, controlling the first peak, while Kch controls refractoriness and the second peak.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93, C128-C129 describe the HH model predictions that match experimental data (Figure 5C vs 5D). The model correctly predicts the differential roles of the two channels and reproduces both wildtype and Kch-mutant phenotypes, providing theoretical support for the two-channel mechanism.

results.result: A 3D agent-based fire-diffuse-fire (ABFDF) model successfully reproduces the experimental wavefront dynamics in 3D biofilms, quantifies anomalous diffusive behavior, and predicts critical biofilm radius for wavefront propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99, C117-C118, and C130 are supported by comparison of simulation results (Figure 7B) with experimental 3D confocal data (Figure 7D, Video 7). The model's ability to predict anomalous exponents and critical size demonstrates its quantitative accuracy.

results.result: Wavefront propagation exhibits anomalous diffusive behavior with curvature effects. Centrifugal waves are superdiffusive subballistic (γ=1.21-1.22), centripetal waves are super-ballistic (γ=2.26-2.43). Critical biofilm size for wavefront initiation is 4.71±0.98 µm (experimental) vs 6.17±1.84 µm (model), much smaller than the 350 µm required for 2D B. subtilis biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C106, C108-C111 are supported by power-law fits to experimental and simulation data (Figure 7C, 7E, Table 1). The anomalous exponents and critical size measurements show good agreement between model and experiment, and the comparison with B. subtilis provides important context.

results.result: The membrane potential dynamics resemble neuronal habituation, where cells show a sustained decrement in response to constant stimulation. This habituation may be involved in the switch to viable but non-culturable phenotype observed with blue light therapy.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 and C140-C141 draw an analogy to neuronal habituation supported by citations, but C143 is explicitly speculative ('We suggest'). While the phenomenological similarity is documented (Figure 6A vs 6B), the mechanistic link to viable-but-non-culturable phenotype lacks direct experimental validation in this study.

results.result: Electrical wavefronts based on potassium ions represent a mechanism for signaling in Gram-negative biofilms, similar to B. subtilis but with differences in frequency, latency, dimensionality, and number of spikes. This may represent a conserved mechanism across biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C119-C120 are supported by the potassium measurements (C75-C76), ion channel genetics (C6-C7), and comparison with cited B. subtilis work. However, C11's claim of 'conserved mechanism' is somewhat speculative as it extrapolates from two species. The core finding of K+-based signaling in E. coli is well-supported.

results.result: ThT is validated as a Nernstian voltage indicator for bacterial membrane potential. Similar dynamics are observed with TMRM, CCCP abolishes spiking, and 10 µM ThT does not affect E. coli growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C41, C43, and C48 provide methodological validation supported by multiple dyes (Appendix 1-figure 1D), CCCP control (Appendix 1-figure 1E), and growth curves (Figure 1F). This establishes the reliability of ThT as a membrane potential reporter in this system.

results.result: The double-peak spiking profile is robust across different light exposure protocols, E. coli strains (DH5α and BW25113), and growth media (LB and M9).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 demonstrate reproducibility across experimental conditions (Appendix 1-figure 1A, 1B, 1C). This strengthens confidence that the observed dynamics are intrinsic to E. coli rather than artifacts of specific experimental conditions.

results.result: Wavefront dynamics are robust across biofilms of different shapes and sizes once biofilms reach appreciable size. The amplitude of action potentials is independent of biofilm density or areal coverage.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by analysis of multiple biofilms (Figure 2C) showing consistent intensity profiles despite morphological variation. This demonstrates the robustness of the electrical signaling phenomenon.

results.result: Wavefront velocity shows expected slow decrease from core to periphery (centrifugal), but centripetal velocity shows unexpected sharp increase near the core, possibly linked to biofilm heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by velocity measurements (Figure 8A, 8B). C112 matches theoretical predictions (Eikonal approximation), while C113 describes an unexpected observation. C114 offers a speculative explanation for the anomalous behavior that requires further investigation.

results.result: The findings suggest potential therapeutic applications: Kch-targeting combined with photodynamic therapy, synergistic effects with electric fields or antibiotics, and improved wound treatments with conducting dressings.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C145-C156 are explicitly speculative predictions about future applications ('predict', 'believe', 'implies', 'could be'). While these are reasonable extrapolations from the findings, they lack experimental validation in this study and represent proposed future work rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: Agent-based modeling provides substantial advantages over classical analytic reaction-diffusion solutions by predicting anomalous wavefront dynamics not captured by traditional approaches, achieving better quantitative agreement with experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C131 and C149 are supported by the demonstrated success of the ABFDF model in predicting anomalous exponents and critical size, which classical solutions cannot capture. The comparison with the N. gonorrhoeae study's analytic approach (C148) provides context for this advantage.

results.result: The model minimally predicts Q = MscK × MscL × MscS for the unknown channel, though the full dependence is likely more complex. The initial spike is key to registering light stress presence.
results.evaluation: Claim C134 explicitly acknowledges uncertainty ('minimally predicts', 'probably more complex'), and C135 is an inference. While the MS channel deletion experiments (C98) support their involvement, the exact relationship between MS channels and the Q channel requires further molecular characterization.

results.result: Background context on biofilms, electrical signaling in bacteria, and the state of knowledge prior to this study, including that robust ion-channel-mediated signaling had not been described in Gram-negative biofilms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29 provide literature context and background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These establish the novelty of the current work by documenting what was previously known about biofilms, bacterial electrophysiology, and the gap in knowledge regarding Gram-negative biofilms.

results.result: The authors claim that ThT acts as a Nernstian voltage indicator in E. coli and use it to measure membrane potential dynamics, showing characteristic spiking patterns in response to blue light. They validate this with TMRM dye and CCCP controls.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers fundamentally challenge the use of ThT as a Nernstian dye in E. coli. Reviewer 2 extensively critiques this, stating 'it is unclear whether the dye used can act as a Nernstian membrane potential dye in E. coli' and notes that 'E. coli cells in the presence of ThT do not load unless there is blue light present.' Reviewer 3 states the authors 'do not share any evidence' for key controls and that 'alternate explanations for and potential confounders of the observed dynamics are not sufficiently addressed.' The reviewers indicate the evidence is incomplete and contradicts previously published work.

results.result: The authors report synchronized membrane potential dynamics with two hyperpolarization peaks in E. coli in response to blue light stress, observed across different strains and growth media.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises fundamental concerns about whether the observed dynamics are actually induced by blue light, stating 'This claim must be supported by the appropriate negative control experiment measuring ThT fluorescence dynamics in the absence of blue light.' The reviewer notes that if no signal is observed without blue light, 'this should be reported in the manuscript—this would be a satisfactory negative control.' Without this control, the causal relationship between blue light and the observed dynamics remains uncertain.

results.result: The authors claim to observe propagating wavefronts of membrane potential that move from the center to the edges of biofilms, then collapse back, followed by a second wavefront emergence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'I cannot identify any traveling wavefronts in the data included in this manuscript.' For cell clusters, the reviewer notes 'I simply do not see any evidence of propagation in either case—rather, all cells get brighter and dimmer in tandem.' Reviewer 1 also 'plotted the spatio-temporal diagram for Video S3 and no electrical propagation is evident at the second peak.' The reviewer concludes 'clear demonstration of these wavefronts is still missing.'

results.result: The authors claim that mechanosensitive ion channels (MscK, MscL, MscS) mediate the first hyperpolarization peak, based on experiments with deletion mutants showing abolished spiking dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes this claim is 'misleading—mechanosensitive ion channels totally ablate membrane potential dynamics, they don't have a specific effect on the first hyperpolarization event.' The reviewer also observes 'the apparent membrane potential is much lower even at the start of the experiment in these mutants—is this expected? This seems to imply that these ion channels also have a blue light-independent effect.' The interpretation of the mutant phenotypes is questioned.

results.result: The authors claim the Kch potassium channel controls the second hyperpolarization peak and refractoriness, based on deletion mutant experiments showing loss of the second peak and complementation restoring dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 requests additional controls, suggesting 'using the ionophore valinomycin at sub-inhibitory concentrations (5 or 10µM). It should abolish the habituation response.' The reviewer also notes 'the Kch complementation experiment exhibits a sharp drop after the first peak but on a single point. It would be more convincing to increase the temporal resolution (1min->10s).' While the basic observation is noted, the mechanistic interpretation requires additional validation.

results.result: The authors claim that Kch-mediated membrane potential dynamics provide photoprotection, showing that Δkch mutants have significantly more cell death (7.6% vs 1.7% PI-positive) after blue light exposure.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'they do not perform the negative control experiment, conducting PI staining for WT and the Δkch mutant in the absence of blue light. In the absence of this control it is not possible to rule out effects of the Δkch mutation on overall viability and/or PI uptake.' Reviewer 1 requests experiments 'without ThT to rule out possible photo-conversion effects on ThT that would modify its toxicity.' Multiple reviewers note that PI uptake can be confounded by membrane potential itself, and alternative viability assays (CFU, outgrowth) are needed.

results.result: The authors show that extracellular potassium ion changes parallel the ThT membrane potential dynamics, suggesting K+ ions play a vital role in the observed dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'the kinetics of the second peak of potassium are different than those observed by ThT (it rises minutes earlier)—is this consistent with the idea that Kch is responsible for that peak? Additionally, the potassium dynamics also include the first ThT peak—is this surprising given that the Kch channel has no effect on this peak according to the model?' The temporal discrepancies raise questions about the interpretation.

results.result: The authors claim that catalase (ROS scavenger) abolishes the second hyperpolarization peak, demonstrating that the membrane potential dynamics is a light stress relief process mediated by ROS.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states this claim is 'not well-supported. There are several possible interpretations of the catalase experiment (which should be discussed); this experiment perhaps suggests that ROS impacts membrane potential but does not indicate that these membrane potential fluctuations help the cells respond to blue light stress.' The reviewer also notes 'this attenuation could alternatively be due to catalase decreasing ThT photobleaching,' and requests photobleaching controls.

results.result: The authors develop a Hodgkin-Huxley model predicting that two voltage-gated ion channels (Q and Kch) with different activation/deactivation kinetics produce the observed double-peak dynamics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 extensively critiques the model, asking 'why n^4 based on that? Why does unknown current have gqz^4 form? Sodium conductance in HH is described by m^3hgNa (again based on detailed conductance measurements), so why unknown current in E.coli by gQz^4? Why leakage is in the form that it is, based on what measurement?' The reviewer emphasizes that in the original HH model, these forms were based on explicit measurements, which are lacking here. Reviewer 1 notes 'the curve in Fig 5D seems to correspond to the biofilm case. Since the model is made for single cells, the curve obtained by the model should be compared with the average curve presented in Fig 1B.'

results.result: The authors develop a 3D agent-based fire-diffuse-fire model that reproduces experimental dynamics, predicts anomalous wavefront diffusion, and calculates a critical biofilm size of ~6 µm for wavefront propagation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'In Fig 7B, the plateau is higher in the simulations than in the biofilm experiments. The authors should add a comment in the paper to explain this discrepancy.' Reviewer 3 states 'I remain unconvinced' about the similarity between model and experiment (Fig S4B vs Fig 7B), 'particularly with respect to the kinetics of the second peak.' The reviewer also notes that 'methods for how these were obtained are not clearly documented' and 'since wavefronts are not evident in the video it is hard to understand what is being measured here.' The model predictions depend on the existence of wavefronts, which reviewers cannot observe.

results.result: The authors show that membrane potential dynamics become more synchronized and faster as cells transition from sparse to microclustered to biofilm configurations, suggesting electrical signaling synchronizes as cells cluster.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 requests that 'histograms of the distributions of time to first peak in both cases should be plotted as a separate figure panel' and that 'statistical significance tests ought to be used to evaluate the statistical strength of the comparisons between these curves.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the way these figures are shown with all traces overlaid at full opacity makes it very difficult to see what is being compared.' The reviewers also note that 'both reviewer 1 and I commented in our initial reviews that the ThT traces, here and elsewhere, should not be normalized.'

results.result: The authors show that the time to first peak decreases with increasing light irradiance, and that a threshold of 15.99 µW/mm² is required for the full two-peak response, suggesting stimulus strength is encoded in the response.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'in the lower irradiance conditions in Fig. 4A, the ThT dynamics are slower overall, and it looks like the ThT intensity is beginning to rise at the end of the measurement' and asks 'could a more prominent second peak be observed in these cases if the measurement time was extended?' The interpretation of the threshold may be confounded by measurement duration. The reviewer also notes 'the analysis and interpretation of the first peak, and particularly of the time-to-fire data is challenging throughout the manuscript the time resolution of the data set is quite limited.'

results.result: The authors claim this is the first report of robust ion-channel-mediated signaling in Gram-negative biofilms, though they acknowledge recent work in N. gonorrhoeae and argue their modeling approach is superior.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 directly contradicts the novelty claim: 'Contrarily to what is stated in the abstract, the group of B. Maier has already reported collective electrical oscillations in the Gram-negative bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Hennes et al., PLoS Biol, 2023).' The claim of being 'first' is factually incorrect.

results.result: The authors show that 10 µM ThT does not affect growth of E. coli strains used in the experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'ThT enhances the photodynamic effects of blue light in E. coli (Bondia et al. 2021 Chemical Communications). The authors could investigate ThT toxicity under these conditions by staining cells with PI after exposing them to blue light with or without ThT staining.' A growth curve alone does not address potential photodynamic toxicity effects during the actual experimental conditions.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate ThT as a membrane potential reporter (C36, C41, C43). OpenEval finds the methodological validation SUPPORTED by multiple dyes and controls. Peer reviewers find it UNSUPPORTED, fundamentally challenging whether ThT acts as a Nernstian dye in E. coli and noting incomplete controls and contradictions with published work.

Both address synchronized membrane potential dynamics and blue light response (C4, C5, C32, C37). OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED by ThT fluorescence data. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether dynamics are actually blue light-induced and noting the absence of critical negative controls (measurements without blue light).

Both evaluate wavefront propagation claims (C49-C54). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by time-lapse microscopy showing bidirectional wavefront movement. Peer reviewers find UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating they cannot identify traveling wavefronts in the data and observe cells brightening in tandem rather than propagating signals.

Both assess mechanosensitive channel roles (C6, C33, C98, C133). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by deletion experiments showing loss of spiking dynamics. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting the claim is misleading as MS channels ablate all dynamics rather than specifically affecting the first peak, and questioning blue light-independent effects.

Both evaluate Kch channel's role in the second peak (C7, C66-C69, C123-C124). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by deletion/complementation experiments. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting additional controls (valinomycin) and noting the complementation data needs better temporal resolution for convincing validation.

Both assess protective role claims via LiveDead assay (C77-C80, C144). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by PI staining showing ~4.5-fold difference. Peer reviewers find UNSUPPORTED, noting absence of critical negative controls (PI staining without blue light, experiments without ThT) and concerns about PI uptake confounds.

Both evaluate potassium measurements (C75-C76). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by IPG-4 indicator showing temporal correlation. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting kinetic discrepancies between potassium and ThT peaks (potassium rises minutes earlier) and questioning consistency with the Kch model.

Both assess catalase experiments linking ROS to second peak (C81-C82). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as mechanistic evidence. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting multiple possible interpretations including catalase reducing ThT photobleaching, and stating the experiment doesn't demonstrate that membrane potential fluctuations help cells respond to stress.

Both evaluate the Hodgkin-Huxley model predictions (C85, C88-C92, C128-C129). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by model matching experimental data. Peer reviewers find UNSUPPORTED, extensively critiquing the lack of empirical basis for model parameters (why n^4, gqz^4 forms) and noting the model should be compared to single-cell rather than biofilm data.

Both assess ABFDF model predictions of anomalous exponents and critical size (C99, C104, C106, C108-C109, C118, C130). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by agreement between simulation and experiment. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting discrepancies in plateau heights, unconvincing similarity in kinetics, and that wavefront measurements are unclear since wavefronts aren't evident in videos.

Both evaluate density-dependent synchronization (C45-C47, C55-C57, C84, C116). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by quantitative measurements showing reduced latency with decreased distance. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, requesting histograms, statistical tests, and noting that overlaid normalized traces make comparisons difficult to evaluate.

Both assess irradiance threshold effects (C71-C74, C138). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by systematic experiments identifying threshold for second peak. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting that slower dynamics at lower irradiance may show second peaks with extended measurement time, and that limited temporal resolution challenges interpretation.

Both address ThT toxicity/growth effects (C48). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by growth curves. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting that growth curves don't address photodynamic toxicity during actual experimental conditions and requesting PI staining experiments with/without ThT under blue light.

Both address novelty claims about Gram-negative bacteria (C149, and C24 in peer review). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED regarding ABFDF model advantages. Peer reviewers find the novelty claim UNSUPPORTED, directly contradicting the 'first' claim by citing Hennes et al. (2023) reporting collective electrical oscillations in N. gonorrhoeae.

Partial overlap on reproducibility across conditions (C38-C40 in OpenEval; C38-C40 also in peer R2). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED demonstrating robustness. Peer reviewers' concerns about blue light controls (R2) indirectly question whether the reproducibility reflects intrinsic dynamics or experimental artifacts.

Both address power-law fits and anomalous exponents (C104, C106, C108-C109). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by agreement between model and experiment. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN (in R10), questioning the model-experiment similarity and noting unclear documentation of measurement methods.
